**E1. (where the wiggles start)** In the **Steady layer** tab, click the lecture grids $P = 1$, $P = 2$ and $P = 5$, and use the slider for $P = 2.5$. For each, note $\rho$ of the central scheme, its minimum value and its maximum error, and compare $\rho$ with the exact growth factor per cell $e^P$. Tick **whole channel** at $P = 5$: how far upstream do the wiggles reach?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer E1"}
$P = 1$ ($\Delta x = 10$ µm): $\rho = 3$ ($e^P = 2.72$), min $c = 0$, error 0.035, no wiggles. $P = 2$ ($\Delta x = 20$ µm): $\rho = \infty$, min $c = 0$, error 0.14: every value copies its upstream neighbour, so the solution is 0 up to the last interior point and then jumps to 1 (a kink, but no negative values). $P = 2.5$ ($\Delta x = 25$ µm): $\rho = -9$, min $c = -0.111$, error 0.19, wiggles. $P = 5$ ($\Delta x = 50$ µm): $\rho = -2.33$ ($e^P = 148$), min $c = -0.429$, error 0.44. The threshold is exactly $P = 2$, where $1 - P/2$ changes sign and $\rho$ jumps from $+\infty$ to negative values. The whole-channel view at $P = 5$ shows the sign alternating all the way to the inlet ($-0.429$, $0.184$, $-0.079$, $0.034$, …), shrinking by a factor $|\rho| = 2.33$ per cell upstream: the oscillation is a property of the discrete equations everywhere, not only at the layer.
:::

**E2. (smooth but smeared)** Stay in **Steady layer**. At $P = 5$, compare the upwind solution (b) with the black and grey curves and read off $D_\text{num}$. Then move the slider to the left until $D_\text{num}$ is below 10 % of $D$. What are $P$, $\Delta x$ and the two maximum errors there? Compare the upwind errors at $P = 0.25$ and $P = 0.125$, and the central errors at the same two grids: which orders do you see?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer E2"}
At $P = 5$ the blue points lie on the grey curve (exact with $D + u\Delta x/2 = 3500$ µm²/s), not on the black one: $D_\text{num} = 2500$ µm²/s $= 2.5\,D$, error 0.16, and no wiggles ($\rho = 6 > 0$). $D_\text{num} = u\Delta x/2 = (P/2)\,D$, so it is below $0.1\,D$ only for $P < 0.2$: the slider gives $P = 0.125$, $\Delta x = 1.25$ µm (400 cells), $D_\text{num} = 62.5$ µm²/s $= 0.063\,D$. There the upwind error is still 0.022, the central error $4.8\times10^{-4}$. From $P = 0.25$ to $0.125$ (halving $\Delta x$) the upwind error goes from 0.042 to 0.022 (halves: first order), the central error from 0.0019 to $4.8\times10^{-4}$ (quarters: second order). Upwind never wiggles, but it needs a much finer grid for the same accuracy.
:::

**E3. (numerical diffusion and the CFL limit in time)** Open **Moving pulse** and click **lecture: Δx 10, C 0.5**. Read the peak the cells see, and compare the blue curve with the black and grey ones. Click **Δx 1** and move $\Delta x$ to 5. Then click **C 0.9** and **C 0.95** (both at $\Delta x = 10$ µm, snapshot $t = 6$ s) and read $C + 2r$ and the range of $c$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer E3"}
Lecture setting: $\Delta t = 0.025$ s, $r = 0.025$, $C + 2r = 0.55$; the cells see a peak of 0.6405 at 10.48 s against the exact 0.975 at 10.50 s. The blue curve lies on the grey one: exact with $D + D_\text{num} = 100 + 500 = 600$ µm²/s. $\Delta x = 5$: peak 0.769 ($D_\text{num} = 250$); $\Delta x = 1$: 0.932 ($D_\text{num} = 50$). The peak time is right in every case; only the height and width are wrong. **C 0.9**: $C + 2r = 0.990$, stable, range 0 … 0.971 at 6 s, peak 0.886 at the cells: a larger time step **reduces** $D_\text{num}$ to $u\Delta x(1 - C)/2 = 100$. **C 0.95**: $C + 2r = 1.045 > 1$, and by $t = 6$ s a zigzag has grown to $-1750$ … $1743$ (the lecture's 1700); at the cells the readout reports a maximum of $1.3\times10^7$. The limit is $C + 2r \le 1$, not $C \le 1$ alone.
:::

**E4. (central differences with explicit time steps)** Tick **central** and click **lecture: Δx 10, C 0.5** again. What happens, and what does the readout say about the condition $C \le 2/P$? (Not derived on this page: for central differences in space with explicit Euler in time, the von Neumann analysis gives stability, for $r \le 1/2$, only when $C^2 \le 2r$, i.e. $u^2\Delta t \le 2D$; with $r = C/P$ this is $C \le 2/P$. The answer below explains it as a negative effective diffusion.) Now lower $C$ to 0.1. Then try $\Delta x = 2$ with $C = 0.5$, and finally **Δx 1**. Note the range of $c$ at $t = 10.5$ s and the peak at the cells for the central scheme each time. Why can the central peak be **higher** than the exact one? Also try $C = 0.9$ at $\Delta x = 1$: which scheme fails now?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer E4"}
At $\Delta x = 10$ µm ($P = 20$), $C = 0.5$ violates $C \le 2/P = 0.1$: the central solution grows to $|c| \approx 10^6$ by 6 s and exceeds $10^{12}$ at 11 s, while upwind with the same $\Delta t$ is stable. At $C = 0.1$ (condition met) it no longer explodes but wiggles: range $-0.339$ … $1.23$ at 10.5 s, peak 1.236 at the cells, against the exact 0.975. $\Delta x = 2$, $C = 0.5$ ($P = 4$, exactly at $C = 2/P$): range $-0.244$ … $1.25$, peak 1.245, wiggles again because $P > 2$. $\Delta x = 1$, $C = 0.5$ ($P = 2$): range 0 … 0.998, no wiggles, peak 0.998 at 10.51 s, higher than the exact 0.975 (upwind gives 0.932). Explicit Euler adds a **negative** numerical diffusion $-u^2\Delta t/2 = -C u\Delta x/2 = -50$ µm²/s, so the central scheme behaves like $D = 50$: too sharp a peak. The condition $C \le 2/P$ is the same as $D - C u\Delta x/2 \ge 0$: the scheme blows up when its effective diffusion coefficient is negative. At $\Delta x = 1$, $C = 0.9$ the roles swap: $r = 0.45$, $C + 2r = 1.8$, and **upwind** blows up within 0.2 s, while central stays bounded (peak 1.000, effective $D = 10$). On a fine grid the diffusion part $2r = 2C/P$ of the condition dominates.
:::

**E5. (the H-filter)** Open **T-sensor / H-filter** and set $L = 2$ mm ($\bar u = 1000$ µm/s). Click the three species and read the fractions in the buffer outlet, the width of the 10–90 % zone at the outlet and where the stream is mixed to 1 %. Compare the small molecule's mixing point with $\bar u w^2/D$ and with the plug-flow estimate $0.42\,\bar u w^2/D$ (Fact 1). Then set $\bar u = 500$ µm/s and $L = 1$ mm: what changes and why?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer E5"}
At 2 mm the buffer outlet receives 47.4 % of the small molecule, 19.3 % of the protein and 0.1 % of the cells (the lecture's 47 %, 19 %, 0.1 %). The 10–90 % zone fills the whole channel for the small molecule, is 45 µm wide for the protein and 1.7 µm for the cells (less than one 2 µm grid cell). The small molecule is mixed to 1 % at about 3.1 mm (3.13 mm with $L = 2$), against $\bar u w^2/D = 10$ mm and $0.42\,\bar u w^2/D = 4.2$ mm for plug flow: with the Poiseuille profile the slow fluid near the walls mixes early, and here that wins. The protein needs 31 mm, ten times longer ($D$ is ten times smaller); the cells 62 m. With $\bar u = 500$ µm/s and $L = 1$ mm every number is the same (47.4 %, 19.3 %, 0.1 %; $Dx/\bar u = 2000$ µm² for the small molecule in both cases) and the mixing point halves to 1.56 mm: only $Dx/\bar u$ matters (B6). A slower flow is a longer channel, at half the throughput.
:::

## Where this leads

- [*Stochastic differential equations*](../sde/lec.qmd) (Part 8): the density of many noisy paths $dX = f\,dt + g\,dW$ obeys the Fokker–Planck equation, an advection–diffusion equation with $u = f$ and $D = g^2/2$, solved there with this flux scheme.
- [*Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation*](../reaction-diffusion/lec.qmd) (unit 35) adds production and degradation terms to the diffusion equation; the explicit/implicit stability rules and grid-refinement checks of this unit carry over.
- The flow profile was **given**. Computing flow fields in real geometries (the Stokes and Navier–Stokes equations) and handling curved walls is the subject of [*Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow*](../fem-outlook/lec.qmd) (Part 11).
- Better advection schemes (higher-order upwind, flux limiters, semi-Lagrangian methods) reduce numerical diffusion without wiggles; we do not cover them. The fit in C6 had one parameter; fitting several (for example $D$ and an unknown inlet concentration) uses the methods of [*Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting*](../nonlinear-least-squares/lec.qmd), and the identifiability problem of B6 is treated in *Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters*.
